look_here_first: Look at young and older branches first: regular corky wings are the signature. Then check that the wings usually stop abruptly at the leaf node, the leaves are pointed, and reproduction is in spring.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Ulmus alata and lists Texas in its native range. Texas regional sources place it in the broader Blackland Prairie/Cross Timbers/Edwards Plateau region, but the prior B012 review did not lock three exact project counties.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Installed for visual learning only; do not count as project-native until exact target-zone county evidence is reconciled.

best_field_traits: regular corky wings commonly present on young and older branches
wings generally terminate abruptly at leaf nodes
flowers before or around leaf-out in spring
morphology_keys.elm_training: Winged elm vs cedar elm: both can have corky wings, but winged elm wings typically stop at the node and reproduction is in spring; cedar elm wings can continue around the node and reproduction is in fall.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Cedar elm has rougher blunter leaves and fall flowers/fruit; American elm has much larger asymmetric leaves and normally unwinged twigs; sweetgum has palmately lobed leaves.
